hero.headline: Federal judge blocks Trump administration immigration restrictions affecting 39 countries
hero.body:
A federal judge ruled Friday that the Trump administration unlawfully barred applicants from 39 travel-ban countries from receiving decisions on asylum applications, work permits, green cards, and citizenship applications.

The decision represents a significant legal setback for the administration's immigration enforcement agenda. The blocked policies had created uncertainty for thousands of people seeking to enter or remain in the United States through legal immigration channels. The restrictions had prevented nationals from countries including Cuba, Haiti, and Venezuela from accessing various forms of immigration relief and humanitarian protections.

The court found that the administration's measures lacked legal authority. Immigration advocates had challenged the restrictions in court, arguing they exceeded executive power and violated procedural requirements. The ruling restores access to immigration benefits for affected nationals while legal challenges continue through the courts.

People from the 39 designated countries can now resume filing applications for asylum, temporary protected status, and other forms of humanitarian relief that had been suspended under the administration's freeze. They will be able to proceed through normal immigration processes.

The timing of the ruling is significant. The Senate passed legislation early Friday morning to fund the Trump administration's controversial immigration crackdown, voting 52-47 to approve $70 billion in funding for US Immigration and Customs Enforcement and the Department of Homeland Security. The vote ended a partial government shutdown that had lasted since February. No Democrats supported the measure.

The administration has not yet announced whether it will appeal the judge's decision. The case is one of several ongoing legal battles over immigration policy changes implemented since the start of Trump's second term. Courts have previously blocked or limited multiple immigration-related executive actions on procedural or constitutional grounds.

The ruling comes as the Trump administration continues efforts to enforce what it calls "mass deportations" of immigrants in the country without authorization. The administration has prioritized what it describes as removing "the worst of the worst" from the country.

According to data obtained by The Guardian through court-ordered records requests, immigration agents filled out deportation forms for thousands of people arrested between fiscal year 2023 and August 2025. The data included biographical details, criminal history, and information about the children of those arrested. The Guardian matched the arrest records with deportation data to track the impact of enforcement actions on families with children under age 18.

The federal judge's decision blocking the restrictions on nationals from the 39 countries marks an important legal challenge to the administration's broader immigration enforcement strategy, even as Congress approved significant new funding for immigration enforcement agencies.

cards.headline: Iran attacks Kuwait airport, killing one in strike near US military base
cards.body:
Iran launched a deadly drone attack on Kuwait International Airport, killing at least one person and wounding 63 others, according to Kuwait's military. The strike damaged a terminal at the airport and marked the first deadly attack in the Gulf region since a ceasefire took effect on April 8.

The assault came as part of an escalating exchange between US and Iranian forces. US Central Command said it had targeted an unladen tanker, the M/T Lexie, in international waters near Kuwait as the vessel moved toward Iran's Kharg Island. An American aircraft fired a missile to disable the tanker's engine after the crew ignored repeated warnings over 24 hours. Iran responded with the drone strike on Kuwait's passenger terminal.

The incident intensified further exchanges of fire. US forces said they had shot down three attack drones launched by Iran toward civilian ships in regional waters. Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps claimed it had attacked the US Fifth Fleet headquarters in Bahrain with missiles and drones in response to the strike on Qeshm Island, though US Central Command denied repelling such an attack. The US military also said it had attacked sites on Qeshm.

Kuwait's defence ministry described the attack as "criminal Iranian aggression which resulted in significant material damage to the building and injuries." Civil aviation authorities suspended traffic and transferred incoming flights to alternative airports. Kuwait's deputy foreign minister summoned Iran's chargé d'affaires to formally protest the attacks and ordered a reduction in Iranian embassy staff, declaring two diplomats persona non grata with 24 hours to leave.

Iran's foreign ministry blamed Kuwait and Bahrain for the strikes, stating they had allowed the United States to use their territory for aggressive plans against Iran. The statement emphasized the responsibility of Kuwait and Bahrain's leaders for "last night's acts of aggression."

The latest escalation jeopardizes ongoing ceasefire negotiations between Washington and Tehran. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio claimed during congressional testimony that war in Iran "is over" and suggested a deal was within reach. However, Trump said in an interview that talks were continuing and he was not seeking escalation, adding that Iran appeared "pretty close" to signing a peace agreement and "it could happen over the weekend."

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu warned that Iran was "playing with fire" and that Trump could order a "full-scale return to military action" if negotiations fail. A military adviser to Iran's supreme leader threatened more missile and drone strikes if the US renewed its attacks, posting that "every shot fired and every attack will be met with a deluge of missiles and drones."

The exchange of strikes demonstrates the fragile state of regional security and the difficulty of achieving diplomatic progress amid active military hostilities.

cards.headline: Putin rejects meeting with Zelensky to discuss ending Ukraine war
cards.teaser: The Russian president dismissed a proposal for face-to-face talks after his Ukrainian counterpart wrote an open letter calling for negotiations.
cards.body:
Russian President Vladimir Putin has rejected Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky's offer for face-to-face talks to discuss ending the war in Ukraine. Speaking at the St. Petersburg economic forum, Putin described Zelensky's open letter as rude and said he sees "no point" in meeting with his Ukrainian counterpart.

Putin reaffirmed Russia's commitment to achieving its war objectives, including seizing all of the eastern Donbas region. Rather than signaling openness to diplomatic resolution, Putin's remarks at the forum suggested Russia intends to continue military operations in Ukraine.

cards.headline: Israel and Hezbollah continue fighting as ceasefire negotiations stall
cards.teaser: Diplomatic efforts to broker a truce between Israel and the Lebanese militant group have not succeeded, leaving Lebanon caught in ongoing conflict.
cards.body:
A ceasefire agreement announced by the United States on Wednesday night has been rejected by Hezbollah, despite being accepted by Israel and Lebanon. The rejection prolongs the conflict between the two sides.

The fighting has put Lebanese civilians at serious risk. A U.N. peacekeeper was killed and others wounded when mortar fire struck the UNIFIL peacekeeping mission in southeastern Lebanon, underscoring the dangers posed by ongoing military operations in the region.

cards.headline: Stock Markets Fall Sharply After Strong Jobs Report Raises Rate Concerns
cards.body:
Global stock markets experienced significant declines this week as concerns about inflated valuations in artificial intelligence companies intensified. The sell-off spread across the US, Asia, and Europe after prominent banking executives warned of a potential market correction following an extended period of record highs.

In the United States, the technology-focused Nasdaq and S&P 500 posted their largest single-day percentage drops in nearly a month. The Nasdaq closed down 2 percent while the S&P 500 fell just over 1 percent, with technology stocks driving much of the decline. The "magnificent seven" AI-related companies, including Nvidia, Amazon, Apple, Microsoft, Tesla, Alphabet, and Meta, all experienced losses. The data analytics company Palantir saw particularly steep declines, falling almost 8 percent despite announcing an improved revenue outlook the previous day.

The market turbulence intensified after investor Michael Burry, known for predicting the 2008 financial crash, took short positions against Palantir and Nvidia. Palantir's chief executive, Alex Karp, criticized Burry and other short-sellers for "trying to call the AI revolution into question." The announcement sparked further selling pressure on these major tech stocks.

Asian markets followed the US declines on Wednesday, recording their sharpest slide in seven months. Stock indices in Japan and South Korea dropped more than 5 percent from their recent record highs. European markets in the UK, France, and Germany also declined slightly on Wednesday morning.

The pessimistic sentiment reflects growing skepticism about artificial intelligence investments. Bank executives from Morgan Stanley and Goldman Sachs cautioned that a market correction could be approaching, joining Jamie Dimon of JP Morgan Chase, who warned in October about the potential for a market crash within six months to two years. Jim Reid, an analyst at Deutsche Bank, noted there was a "growing chorus discussing whether we might be on the verge of an equity correction," adding that "the last 24 hours have brought a clear risk-off move, as concerns over lofty tech valuations have hit investor sentiment."

Some analysts have questioned the returns on artificial intelligence investments, pointing out that the vast majority of AI spending has concentrated on a small group of technology companies, particularly OpenAI and Nvidia, with limited results so far.

The market turmoil also extended to other risk assets. Bitcoin briefly dipped below $100,000 for the first time since June as investors moved money away from riskier investments. Bitcoin had reached a record high above $126,000 in early October but declined 3.7 percent that month, marking its worst monthly performance in the last decade.

The broad sell-off underscores heightened investor anxiety about whether recent market gains have outpaced fundamental value in technology and AI-related companies.

cards.headline: Employers Add 172,000 Jobs in May as Hiring Pace Stays Strong
cards.teaser: The labor market extended its recent hiring momentum despite wage growth lagging inflation and persistent consumer pessimism.
cards.body:
Employers added 172,000 jobs in May, with the unemployment rate holding steady at 4.3%. The figure exceeded economist predictions of 80,000 new jobs, and prior months saw significant upward revisions—March and April figures were boosted by 93,000 combined. Job growth occurred across multiple sectors, including restaurants, bars and hotels.

Despite strong hiring, wage gains have softened and failed to keep pace with rising prices, continuing to pressure workers' purchasing power. The robust jobs report triggered a sharp market sell-off, with the S&P 500 falling more than 2 percent as investors anticipated higher interest rates ahead.

cards.headline: House panel advances $1.15 trillion defense bill with Hegseth oversight measures
cards.teaser: The House Armed Services Committee passed a defense policy bill that includes new accountability requirements for the defense secretary.
cards.body:
The House Armed Services Committee advanced a defense policy bill early Friday that would authorize $1.15 trillion for the Pentagon. The legislation includes a pay increase for service members and supports U.S. allies and acquisition reforms.

The bill contains measures requiring additional accountability from Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. The oversight provisions drew some bipartisan support on the committee. The legislation represents one of the largest defense policy bills in recent history.

cards.headline: France opens investigation into alleged Israeli mistreatment of Gaza flotilla activists
cards.teaser: Activists detained while trying to reach Gaza have accused Israeli authorities of abuse during custody, claims Israel has denied.
cards.body:
French authorities have opened an investigation into the treatment of pro-Palestinian activists detained by Israel after attempting to reach Gaza by sea. The activists claim they were abused while in Israeli custody. Israeli authorities have denied the mistreatment allegations.

The flotilla was intercepted while trying to reach the Gaza Strip. France's decision to launch an investigation suggests the case involves French citizens or that the allegations warrant official scrutiny.

cards.headline: European Union says Montenegro could join by 2028
cards.teaser: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the Balkan nation is within reach of membership after a summit on EU expansion.
cards.body:
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said Montenegro could join the European Union by 2028 following a summit on Balkans expansion. The statement underscores the EU's advancing plans to bring new members into the bloc.

At the summit, Germany and France advocated for faster benefits for EU candidates in the Balkans and Moldova. Among Balkan hopefuls seeking membership, Montenegro is positioned closest to achieving full EU status.

cards.headline: Sherpa survives six days alone on Everest, family says he was abandoned
cards.teaser: Dawa Sherpa, 57, was found alive after nearly a week missing on the world's tallest mountain, sustained by chocolate and ice.
cards.body:
Dawa Sherpa, a 57-year-old mountain guide, was found alive by a cleaning crew on Mount Everest nearly six days after he went missing. He survived the ordeal by eating chocolate and chewing ice while slowly descending the mountain. Speaking to the BBC from his hospital bed, Sherpa described his experience during the challenging period alone.

His wife has expressed concern that more could have been done to locate him sooner, suggesting inadequate rescue efforts were made during his absence. The discovery came after he had been missing for almost a week on the world's tallest mountain.

cards.headline: Astronauts shelter in spacecraft during air leak repair attempt on space station
cards.teaser: NASA directed crew members to board a spacecraft as a safety measure while Russian cosmonauts worked to fix a leak in a tunnel area.
cards.body:
NASA ordered five astronauts aboard the International Space Station to enter their docked Crew Dragon spacecraft and don spacesuits as a precautionary measure on Friday morning. The evacuation alert came after Russian specialists detected two air leaks while pressurizing the transfer chamber of the Zveza module's Russian segment.

NASA reversed the evacuation order after the repair attempt concluded, and the astronauts returned to normal operations. The crew—four members of NASA's Crew-12 mission including two US astronauts, a French astronaut and a Russian cosmonaut—remained safely sheltered during the repair work in the tunnel area of the station.

cards.headline: Trump withdraws Pulte nomination for intelligence director after Senate opposition
cards.teaser: President Trump confirmed he will not nominate Bill Pulte for director of national intelligence after three Republican senators voted to bar him from serving temporarily.
cards.body:
President Trump confirmed he instructed Bill Pulte to remove intelligence community employees, arguing that staffing levels were "way too high." Pulte, a Trump loyalist with no prior intelligence experience, was initially appointed as a temporary director of national intelligence but will not be nominated for the permanent role after Senate opposition emerged.

The president said Pulte is "less shackled" in his temporary capacity to make significant personnel changes across federal intelligence agencies. Meanwhile, the administration's separate effort to restructure mortgage giants Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac faces new uncertainty following the personnel turmoil surrounding the intelligence leadership transition.

cards.headline: Illinois governor suspends tax breaks for data centers
cards.teaser: Governor JB Pritzker announced a pause on tax incentives offered to data centers operating in Illinois.
cards.body:
Illinois Governor JB Pritzker has suspended tax breaks for data center companies operating in the state. The decision halts processing of new applications for the incentive program, which was created to attract technology infrastructure investment to Illinois.

Pritzker's move comes as policymakers nationwide reconsider data center policies. New York's legislature recently passed a one-year moratorium on large new data centers, citing concerns about environmental impact and energy prices. Illinois's governor indicated he wants additional discussion about the state's incentive program before approving new agreements.

cards.headline: Virginia man sentenced to life in prison for double murder plot with au pair
cards.teaser: Brendan Banfield received a life sentence for an elaborate scheme with a Brazilian au pair to kill his wife.
cards.body:
A Virginia man was sentenced to life in prison for plotting with an au pair to murder his wife in a double-murder scheme. Brendan Banfield had an affair with the Brazilian au pair and together they carried out the plan to eliminate his wife.

The case involved two deaths as part of the elaborate plot. Prosecutors presented evidence showing Banfield and the au pair worked together to execute the murders, which allowed Banfield to escape his marriage while avoiding divorce proceedings.

cards.headline: Murder trial begins in fatal stabbing at Texas high school track meet
cards.teaser: Jurors watched videos of the stabbing incident and saw the knife allegedly used in the death of Austin Metcalf at a Frisco ISD track meet.
cards.body:
The murder trial of Karmelo Anthony began with prosecutors arguing the fatal stabbing of Austin Metcalf at a Texas track meet was murder, not self-defense. Jurors were shown videos of the stabbing incident and viewed the knife prosecutors say was used in the attack.

The case centers on whether Anthony acted in self-defense when he stabbed Metcalf at the Frisco ISD athletic event. Opening statements laid out competing narratives, with the prosecution asserting the killing was intentional murder while the defense is expected to argue Anthony feared for his safety.

cards.headline: British actor Anthony Head dies at 72
cards.teaser: The actor known for roles in Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Ted Lasso died from complications of pneumonia.
cards.body:
Anthony Head, the British actor best known for playing Rupert Giles in Buffy the Vampire Slayer, has died at 72 from complications related to pneumonia. He also starred in Ted Lasso, Merlin, and Little Britain.

Head first became a household name in the 1980s through his appearances in Nescafe coffee advertisements, which launched a decades-long television career across British and American productions.

cards.headline: Everest guide rescued after six days on mountain
cards.teaser: Dawa Sherpa survived by eating chocolate and chewing ice before a cleaning crew spotted him sliding down Mount Everest.
cards.body:
A Mount Everest guide survived six days stranded on the mountain by eating chocolate and chewing ice. Dawa Sherpa was discovered by a cleaning crew working on the slopes as he made his way down.

After his rescue, Sherpa spoke to the BBC from a hospital bed about his ordeal on the world's tallest mountain.

cards.headline: Trump to Meet AI Company Leaders on Government Investment Plans
cards.teaser: The president said he expects to meet leaders of top artificial intelligence companies next week to discuss US investment.
cards.body:
President Trump announced on Friday that he plans to meet with leaders of major artificial intelligence companies next week. The meetings will focus on potential US government investment in their operations.

The Trump administration has been discussing possible government stakes in AI startups including OpenAI. Reports indicate the talks center on government profit-sharing arrangements with artificial intelligence firms. The meetings represent a potential shift in how the federal government engages with the AI industry.

cards.headline: States Prepare Legal Challenge to Block Paramount-Warner Bros Merger
cards.teaser: Multiple US states are preparing a lawsuit to stop Paramount's acquisition of Warner Bros, according to sources.
cards.body:
Several US states are preparing legal action to block Paramount's proposed acquisition of Warner Bros, sources told Reuters. California is expected to decide soon whether it will join efforts to challenge the deal.

Paramount's top lawyer said some opposition to the Warner Bros deal stems from antisemitism. The merger faces scrutiny over potential competitive concerns in the entertainment industry. States typically file antitrust lawsuits when they believe mergers will harm consumers or reduce market competition.

cards.headline: S&P 500 Rejects SpaceX Entry, Blocking OpenAI and Anthropic
cards.teaser: The index operator reaffirmed existing rules that prevent SpaceX from early entry into its benchmark index.
cards.body:
S&P Dow Jones Indices will not change its rules to allow SpaceX into its benchmark S&P 500 index early. The decision also blocks potential early entry for other private companies including OpenAI and Anthropic.

SpaceX had sought inclusion despite not meeting standard requirements for publicly traded companies. The index operator reaffirmed that existing eligibility rules remain in place. The decision demonstrates the power of index gatekeepers in determining which companies can access benchmark status and the passive investment flows that accompany it.

cards.headline: Young Graduates Struggle in Job Market Despite Overall Improvement
cards.teaser: People entering the workforce face harder times starting careers, a pattern that has produced permanent effects in past economic periods.
cards.body:
The labor market showed resilience in May, with U.S. employers adding 172,000 jobs while the unemployment rate remained at 4.3%. The figures exceeded economist expectations of 80,000 new jobs, and previous months saw significant upward revisions—March and April job additions were revised up by a combined 93,000.

However, this broad employment strength masks challenges for young workers entering the job market. Early-career difficulties can create lasting effects, with workers who start during weak conditions typically earning less and advancing more slowly than those beginning during stronger periods. The current struggle for new graduates contrasts sharply with the overall labor market's vigor.

cards.headline: Semiconductor Stocks Lead Broader Tech Decline
cards.teaser: Chip stocks headed for their worst day of 2026 as the broader technology sector sold off sharply.
cards.body:
Semiconductor stocks experienced their worst day of 2026 on Friday, dragging down major technology indexes. The Nasdaq fell sharply alongside declines in the S&P 500 and Dow Jones Industrial Average, which dropped more than 550 points following the U.S. jobs report.

The semiconductor sector's selloff contributed significantly to the broader market pullback. Treasury yields also jumped during the trading session as investors reassessed economic conditions.

hero.headline: Google agrees to pay SpaceX $920 million monthly for computing capacity
hero.body:
Google and SpaceX announced a deal on Friday under which Google will pay SpaceX $920 million per month for computing services. The agreement comes one week before SpaceX's scheduled initial public offering, marking a significant corporate partnership between two major technology companies.

The monthly payment represents one of the largest cloud computing contracts announced in recent years. The deal positions SpaceX to provide substantial computing infrastructure to Google, though the companies did not disclose the specific services or duration of the agreement. The timing suggests both companies see strategic value in finalizing the arrangement before SpaceX becomes a publicly traded entity.

SpaceX has been building out computing capabilities alongside its satellite internet service Starlink, which operates thousands of satellites in low Earth orbit. The company has invested heavily in ground infrastructure and data centers to support its space operations and communications network. This agreement with Google represents a new revenue stream for SpaceX beyond its traditional launch services and Starlink subscriptions.

The announcement comes as SpaceX prepares for what is expected to be one of the most closely watched public offerings in recent memory. The company, founded by Elon Musk, has grown from a startup rocket manufacturer into a dominant force in the space industry, with contracts from NASA, the Department of Defense, and commercial customers worldwide. The Google deal adds to SpaceX's revenue base ahead of its debut on public markets.

For Google, the agreement secures access to computing capacity at a time when demand for cloud infrastructure continues to grow, driven in part by artificial intelligence applications. The deal also represents a bet on SpaceX's infrastructure capabilities beyond its core space transportation business. Both companies have significant operations and investments in advanced technology, making the partnership a convergence of space, communications, and computing infrastructure.

cards.headline: S&P 500 declines to waive profitability rule for SpaceX ahead of IPO
cards.teaser: The index committee will not grant SpaceX early entry into the benchmark, limiting access to passive investment funds.
cards.body:
The S&P 500 index committee has decided against waiving its profitability requirement for SpaceX, preventing the aerospace company from gaining fast-track entry into the benchmark index. This means SpaceX will miss out on the substantial capital flows from passive investors who track the S&P 500.

The ruling applies to unprofitable companies across sectors, including those in artificial intelligence that had similarly requested exceptions. SpaceX is preparing for its initial public offering next week, though the index committee maintained its standard profitability standards despite the company's prominence in the aerospace industry.

cards.headline: Data center developer cuts project size by half after local opposition
cards.teaser: A developer scaled back plans for a large data center facility following community protests.
cards.body:
A data center developer has reduced the size of a planned facility by 50 percent following sustained protests from local residents. The developer said the company felt it had no choice but to shrink the project in response to the opposition.

The developer described feeling beaten up by the process and said the community reaction left few alternatives. The original data center plans drew objections that ultimately forced the compromise. Data centers have become points of tension in some communities due to their power consumption, water usage, and infrastructure demands.

cards.headline: General Motors accelerates new battery technology deployment to cut electric vehicle costs
cards.teaser: GM aims to introduce new battery tech up to a year ahead of schedule to reduce EV prices.
cards.body:
General Motors is accelerating the rollout of new battery technology by up to a year to reduce electric vehicle prices and gain a competitive advantage. A specific manufacturing facility is central to this strategy.

The facility will be instrumental in scaling production of the new batteries to meet GM's volume targets and support the company's broader effort to make EVs more affordable.

cards.headline: Supabase doubles valuation to $10 billion in eight months
cards.teaser: The open source database company has grown rapidly with help from AI coding tools.
cards.body:
Supabase has reached a $10 billion valuation, doubling its worth in just eight months. The company demonstrates how an open source project can evolve into a fast-growing commercial enterprise in the competitive database and backend services market.

The company's rapid growth has been fueled by AI-powered development tools including Claude and Codex, which have accelerated software development workflows and contributed to increased adoption of Supabase's services.

cards.headline: Astronauts return to International Space Station after air leak repair attempt
cards.teaser: Five crew members sheltered in place during a Russian effort to fix a leak in a tunnel area.
cards.body:
Astronauts aboard the International Space Station have resumed normal duties after being placed on evacuation alert due to an air leak. NASA ordered five crew members—including two US astronauts, a French astronaut and a Russian cosmonaut from the Crew-12 mission—to enter their docked Crew Dragon spacecraft and don spacesuits as a precaution.

Russian specialists discovered two air leaks while pressurising the transfer chamber of the Zveda module. After repair attempts paused, NASA gave the all-clear for crew members to return to regular activities aboard the orbiting laboratory.

cards.headline: FBI and Google warn of ransomware gang sending fake IT workers to victim offices
cards.teaser: Criminals posing as tech support have stolen data from law firms using USB drives and remote tools.
cards.body:
Google and the FBI have warned of a ransomware group called Silent Ransom Group that uses an unusual tactic: sending people posing as IT support workers to target organizations in person. These fake IT employees have visited law firm offices, where they steal data using USB drives or remote access tools.

This physical approach to cybercrime sets the group apart from typical remote attacks. Law firms are attractive targets because they hold valuable client information that can be exploited for ransom demands.

hero.headline: NCAA rules four former Alabama State players fixed game outcome
hero.teaser: The hero of Alabama State's first NCAA tournament win and three teammates were permanently banned for accepting payments from gamblers to fix a game result.
hero.body:
The NCAA has announced that four former Alabama State basketball players from the 2024-25 team have been ruled permanently ineligible after accepting payment from gamblers to fix the outcome of a game during that season.

The ruling affects the player who scored the winning basket in Alabama State's first NCAA tournament victory, along with three of his teammates. All four players are now barred from any future NCAA competition.

The decision represents one of the most significant game-fixing cases in recent college basketball history. The NCAA's announcement did not specify which game was targeted or provide details about the amounts of payment involved in the scheme.

Game-fixing scandals have periodically emerged in college basketball over the years, but cases involving multiple players from the same team remain relatively uncommon. The involvement of the player who delivered the decisive moment in Alabama State's tournament breakthrough adds another layer to the case, as it raises questions about the integrity of a historic moment for the program.

The NCAA's investigation uncovered evidence that the players accepted money from individuals with gambling interests to manipulate the outcome of at least one game during the 2024-25 season. The organization's enforcement process ultimately determined that the players violated NCAA rules regarding amateurism and ethical conduct.

Permanent ineligibility represents the NCAA's most severe penalty for student athletes. It prevents players from competing in any NCAA-sanctioned sport for the remainder of their collegiate careers and eliminates their ability to transfer to other NCAA institutions while maintaining eligibility.

The ruling does not appear to have resulted in additional penalties against Alabama State University itself at this time, though the NCAA sometimes takes additional action against institutions in game-fixing cases depending on whether they determine that the school failed in its compliance responsibilities.

The case underscores ongoing concerns about the intersection of gambling and college athletics. As sports betting has expanded across the United States in recent years, colleges and the NCAA have heightened efforts to educate athletes about the dangers of associating with gamblers and the serious consequences of attempting to fix games.

The NCAA has strict rules prohibiting athletes from engaging with gambling operations in any capacity that could compromise the integrity of competition. Even accepting payment to lose intentionally or manipulate game outcomes by specific margins violates these standards and triggers permanent ineligibility.

The announcement serves as a reminder of the NCAA's commitment to maintaining competitive integrity, though it also highlights challenges the organization faces in policing athlete conduct off the court. The case involves players who sought financial benefit through illegal gambling schemes rather than through authorized compensation channels available to athletes.

cards.headline: NASCAR Hall of Famer Ned Jarrett dies at 93
cards.teaser: NASCAR Hall of Famer Ned Jarrett died Thursday at his home in Newton, North Carolina, his family announced.
cards.body:
NASCAR Hall of Famer Ned Jarrett died Thursday at his home in Newton, North Carolina, his family announced. He was 93. The two-time Cup Series champion passed away peacefully of natural causes.

Jarrett won back-to-back NASCAR Grand National Series championships in 1961 and 1965, establishing himself among the sport's early legends. After retiring from driving, he became a prominent broadcaster for CBS, ESPN, and other networks, helping grow NASCAR's audience during the sport's expansion. He was inducted into the NASCAR Hall of Fame in 2011.

cards.headline: Bears advance stadium plans in Hammond, Indiana
cards.teaser: The Chicago Bears moved closer to leaving the city after the team's board of directors voted to advance stadium development plans in nearby Hammond, Indiana.
cards.body:
The Bears took a significant step toward leaving Chicago after the team's board of directors voted Thursday to advance their stadium development plans in Hammond, Indiana. The move brings the franchise closer to ending its long history in Chicago, where it has played since 1921.

Hammond is located in Northwest Indiana, just across the state line from Illinois. The potential relocation would represent a major shift for one of the NFL's oldest franchises.

cards.headline: Buccaneers quarterback Baker Mayfield says contract talks stalled
cards.teaser: Baker Mayfield said contract extension negotiations with the Buccaneers are not meeting his expectations and that it is time to finalize a long-term deal.
cards.body:
Buccaneers quarterback Baker Mayfield said contract extension talks with the team "are not anywhere close to what we were thinking" and stressed it's "time to get something done long-term." The comments came during his first public remarks of the offseason.

Mayfield is seeking a long-term deal as he enters a crucial season as the team's starting quarterback.

cards.headline: FIFA cancels 60 World Cup tickets issued for free by website error
cards.teaser: FIFA canceled World Cup tickets given to approximately 60 fans who received them at no cost due to a website malfunction.
cards.body:
FIFA has canceled World Cup tickets that were mistakenly issued for free to approximately 60 fans due to a website error. The tickets were allocated at no charge because of a payment processing issue during checkout.

FIFA is now asking the affected fans to purchase the tickets at full price. The governing body said it "regrets" the technical glitch. The ticketing process is currently being investigated by attorneys general.

cards.headline: US coach Pochettino frustrated as Chris Richards ruled out of final World Cup tuneup
cards.teaser: United States coach Mauricio Pochettino expressed frustration after first-choice center back Chris Richards was ruled out of the team's last friendly before the World Cup with an ankle injury.
cards.body:
United States coach Mauricio Pochettino expressed frustration after Chris Richards was ruled out of the team's final World Cup warmup friendly against Germany due to an ankle injury. The defender's participation in the tournament itself now remains uncertain as Pochettino awaits further medical assessments.

Richards has been a key starter in Pochettino's defensive lineup. The timing of the injury is problematic for the USMNT as they prepare for the World Cup, and Pochettino indicated dissatisfaction with how the injury assessment had been handled.

cards.headline: Maple Leafs GM says Auston Matthews committed despite exit speculation
cards.teaser: Toronto general manager John Chayka said he is not concerned about speculation that team captain Auston Matthews wants to leave the Maple Leafs.
cards.body:
Maple Leafs general manager John Chayka dismissed recent speculation that captain Auston Matthews is seeking an exit from Toronto, expressing confidence in the star player's commitment to the team.

The franchise's leading player has faced questions about his long-term future in Toronto following the circulating reports of a potential departure.

hero.headline: Anthony Head, actor known for Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Ted Lasso, dies at 72
hero.body:
Anthony Head, the British actor best known for playing Rupert Giles in Buffy the Vampire Slayer, has died at age 72. He passed away peacefully from complications due to pneumonia, surrounded by his family, according to a statement from his daughters Emily and Daisy Head.

"It has been, and forever will be, an honour and a privilege to be his daughters, and to have witnessed first-hand the impact both he and his work have had on so many," they said.

Head's most iconic role came as the mentor and Watcher to Sarah Michelle Gellar's character throughout Buffy the Vampire Slayer's seven-season run. In the show, Giles served as the school librarian at Sunnydale High School and became a beloved father figure to the main character. Gellar paid tribute to Head on Instagram, beginning with a quote from her character: "Tell Giles I figured it out and I'm ok." She then wrote, "Well I don't have it figured out and I'm not ok. But I know I'm the lucky one because I knew you."

Beyond Buffy, Head built a diverse career spanning theatre, television, and film. He was born in Camden, London, to artistic parents. His father was a documentary filmmaker who founded Verity Films, and his mother was an actress who appeared in the 1960s BBC crime drama Maigret. Head's early passion for performance led him to begin his professional career on stage, including starring in a 1978 West End revival of Godspell.

Head appeared in film roles including The Iron Lady and The Inbetweeners Movie. On television, he had a recurring role in the BBC sketch comedy Little Britain, playing a British prime minister constantly fawned over by an assistant. He also appeared in the BBC fantasy series Merlin.

More recently, Head joined the cast of Apple TV's Ted Lasso, where he played Rupert Mannion, a former football club owner. He regularly appeared in scenes with co-creator Jason Sudeikis, and the pair received praise for their on-screen chemistry.

Despite his rise to global fame, Head maintained perspective about celebrity. He told the Guardian that his success taught him "not to get caught up in the hype," noting that while some co-stars competed for magazine covers, he preferred to focus on his work.

During the filming of Buffy the Vampire Slayer, Head spent five years based in Los Angeles while his partner Sarah and their two young daughters remained in England. He made frequent trips home, arranging his shooting schedule to allow for regular visits.

His daughters expressed that while their grief is profound, "we know his legacy will live on in the shows he was a part of and in the audiences that love them. How lucky we are to know we are able to watch him doing what he loved, even when he is no longer with us."

cards.headline: Taylor Swift releases music video for Toy Story 5 song
cards.teaser: The singer released a video for her original contribution to the animated film, featuring footage focused on the character Jessie.
cards.body:
Taylor Swift released the music video for "I Knew It, I Knew You," an original country-influenced song she wrote for Toy Story 5. The video consists entirely of footage from the Toy Story films and focuses on the character Jessie, who inspired the composition.

Swift acknowledged the legacy of Randy Newman's iconic Toy Story songs, calling them "incomparable" and crediting him with creating the film series' musical world. Her contribution marks a notable entry into soundtrack work, building on her previous film music collaborations.

cards.headline: Paramount unveils CBS late night and 60 Minutes changes at upfront presentation
cards.teaser: The company held its first upfront event under CEO David Ellison, showcasing programming changes to advertising executives.
cards.body:
Paramount Skydance held an upfront presentation in New York City in late April, the first since CEO David Ellison took control. Advertising and media buying executives attended to review the company's programming offerings and assess Paramount's pitch for the coming season.

The presentation included announcements about changes to CBS late night programming and 60 Minutes. Recent upheaval at the news magazine prompted correspondents Lesley Stahl, Bill Whitaker, and Jon Wertheim to announce they would remain at the program, stating they didn't want to see "60 Minutes die" despite the turmoil from recent staff departures.

cards.headline: Madonna to premiere Confessions II film at Tribeca Festival before YouTube release
cards.teaser: The film, directed by David Toro and Solomon Chase, will debut at the Beacon Theatre before streaming online.
cards.body:
Madonna announced that Confessions II The Film will have its world premiere at the Tribeca Film Festival at New York City's Beacon Theatre. The film is directed by David Toro and Solomon Chase.

Following the theatrical premiere, the film will be released on YouTube on June 8 at 11 a.m. ET. The dual release strategy allows for both a festival debut and wide digital availability within days of the premiere screening.

cards.headline: Judge denies Marilyn Manson's motion to dismiss assault lawsuit
cards.teaser: The musician's latest attempt to have his former assistant's sexual assault case thrown out was rejected by the court.
cards.body:
A judge has rejected Marilyn Manson's attempt to dismiss a sexual assault lawsuit filed by a former assistant. The court denied the motion, allowing the case to proceed. The judge expressed reluctance to dismiss the case so quickly after it had been revived, saying he would have difficulty sleeping if he granted the dismissal at this stage.

The lawsuit alleges sexual assault by the musician. The case had previously been dismissed before being brought back to court, and this latest effort by Manson to have it thrown out has now failed.

cards.headline: Netflix says it will not work with directors seeking theatrical releases
cards.teaser: The streaming company's film chief outlined the platform's position on theatrical distribution, despite recent exceptions.
cards.body:
Netflix's film leadership has stated the company won't partner with directors who prioritize theatrical releases. A Netflix film executive made the declaration, acknowledging the streaming service has accepted this constraint on its filmmaker relationships.

The position contrasts with Netflix's recent theatrical ambitions. The company has been signaling openness to cinema partnerships and has made overtures to movie theaters, even after its bid to acquire Warner Bros. collapsed.

cards.headline: Phoebe Bridgers plays Madison Square Garden show with phone ban
cards.teaser: The singer-songwriter returned to the New York venue for what was described as her biggest concert in years.
cards.body:
Phoebe Bridgers performed at Madison Square Garden in her largest show in several years. The concert marked a significant milestone for the singer-songwriter, who has cultivated a dedicated fanbase over the past decade.

The venue implemented a phone ban during the performance, requiring attendees to put away their devices. The policy created a more focused concert experience, allowing the audience to engage fully with the live music without digital distractions.

hero.headline: House panel advances $1.15 trillion defense bill with Hegseth oversight measures
hero.teaser: The House Armed Services Committee passed a defense policy bill that includes new accountability requirements for the defense secretary.
hero.body:
The House Armed Services Committee advanced a defense policy bill early Friday that would authorize $1.15 trillion for the Pentagon. The legislation includes a pay increase for service members and supports U.S. allies and acquisition reforms.

The bill contains measures requiring additional accountability from Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. The oversight provisions drew some bipartisan support on the committee. The legislation represents one of the largest defense policy bills in recent history.

cards.headline: Senate passes $69.5 billion immigration enforcement funding through 2029
cards.teaser: The Senate approved a budget reconciliation package funding immigration enforcement operations after an overnight session.
cards.body:
The Senate passed a $69.5 billion immigration enforcement funding bill early Friday morning after an overnight voting session. The legislation funds immigration enforcement operations through 2029.

The bill's passage came after weeks of delays stemming from controversy over an unrelated $1.776 billion settlement fund. The Senate proceeded without imposing new limits on that settlement fund, which had threatened to block the legislation entirely.

cards.headline: ICE ends public reporting of deaths among recently released detainees
cards.teaser: U.S.
cards.body:
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement will stop publicly reporting deaths of detainees who die shortly after being released from custody, according to an internal memo from acting ICE Director David Venturella. The change rescinds a 2021 Biden-era policy that required the agency to report deaths occurring within 30 days of release to Congress and investigate them.

Venturella described the policy change as "common sense" but did not provide detailed reasoning. The shift removes a key source of data that advocacy groups and oversight bodies have used to assess detention conditions and identify potential systemic health problems within ICE facilities.

cards.headline: Trump administration auctions Alaska wildlife refuge drilling rights, draws minimal interest
cards.teaser: Only two companies bid on a small fraction of land tracts opened for oil and gas leasing in an Alaskan refuge.
cards.body:
Original Card Text (Unchanged)

The Trump administration auctioned off drilling rights in an Alaska wildlife refuge Friday, but the lease sale attracted only two bidders. Of approximately 60 tracts of land opened for leasing, only five received bids.

HEX Energy and the state of Alaska were the only entities to submit bids on the available tracts. The limited response suggests minimal commercial interest in drilling in the refuge despite the administration making the land available for energy development.

---

Reasoning: The additional source material provided covers unrelated Trump administration actions (civil rights investigations at universities and efforts to modify the Roadless Rule for national forests). Neither article discusses the Alaska wildlife refuge drilling auction, so the original card text should remain unchanged per your instructions.

cards.headline: Trump calls Senator Thom Tillis a loser over attorney general nomination dispute
cards.teaser: The president criticized the North Carolina Republican who threatened to oppose Todd Blanche's nomination over January 6 comments.
cards.body:
President Trump criticized Sen. Thom Tillis on Friday, calling him "a loser" after the North Carolina Republican threatened to oppose Todd Blanche's nomination as Attorney General. Tillis said he would withhold support unless Blanche condemns the January 6 Capitol attacks.

Trump told reporters that Tillis chose not to seek reelection because Trump would not back him. The dispute reflects broader tensions between the president and some Senate Republicans over both executive nominations and the party's stance on January 6.

cards.headline: Measles cases in U.S. surpass 2,000 for the year
cards.teaser: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention confirmed more than 2,000 measles cases so far in 2026, approaching last year's total.
cards.body:
The number of measles cases in the United States has exceeded 2,000 this year, quickly approaching the full annual total from last year. As of June 4, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention confirmed 2,030 cases in 2026.

Ninety-three percent of the cases, or 1,890, are associated with outbreaks. The rapid accumulation of cases in just the first five months of the year indicates the disease is spreading at a faster rate than in 2025.

cards.headline: Deb Haaland wins New Mexico Democratic primary for governor
cards.teaser: The former Biden administration official could become the first female Native American governor if elected in November.
cards.body:
Deb Haaland, who served in President Biden's administration, won the Democratic primary for New Mexico governor. The victory positions her for the general election in November.

If elected, Haaland would make history as the first female Native American governor in the United States. She will face the Republican nominee in the fall campaign.
